column1: # THE ENCODINGS: encode(s, name) writes a string's UTF-8 bytes as text,
# and decode(t, name) reads them back as a string. The names are a closed
# set: base64 and base64url of RFC 4648, the first with its padding and
# the second without, and hex in lowercase.
# Every expectation below is what BOTH engines answer. A host library
# would answer most of these differently in each port: one decoder skips
# line breaks, another takes missing padding or stray low bits, and one
# writes base64url with padding where the other writes none. So both
# ports spell each encoding out by hand, and these rows hold them to the
# base64 is RFC 4648 section 4: three bytes to four characters, and a
# last group of one or two bytes padded with `=` to four.
# base64url is section 5: `-` and `_` where base64 writes `+` and `/`,
# and no padding, as a token and aontu's own hashes are written.
# hex is two lowercase digits a byte.
# An encoding acts on the UTF-8 bytes, so a character is one to four of
# The arguments are values like any other: computed, referenced, or
# hex is read in either case, the one place decode takes more than
# decode(encode(s, n), n) is s, for every string and each name.

column3: o: decode(encode("日本語 😀 é", base64), base64)
o: decode(encode("日本語 😀 é", base64url), base64url)
o: decode(encode("日本語 😀 é", hex), hex)

column1: # And encode(decode(t, n), n) is t wherever decode answers, hex in
# uppercase aside: base64 text has one spelling for its bytes.
# A byte below U+0080 is a character, the first of them too.
# A NAME THAT IS NO ENCODING IS REFUSED, `encode_name`: the set is
# closed, and a name is matched as it is written.

column4: was given a name that is no encoding

column1: # TEXT THE ENCODING COULD NOT HAVE WRITTEN IS REFUSED,
# `decode_malformed`. base64 without its padding, with too much, or
# with it anywhere but the end.
# A character outside the alphabet, a space and a line break among
# them, and the other alphabet's two.
# Low bits a last character holds beyond its bytes: `aA==` is the one
# spelling of its byte, and `aG==` is not one.
# hex with half a byte, or a character that is no digit.
# And text whose bytes are not UTF-8: a string holds characters, so
# binary data stays in its encoded form.

column4: was given text the encoding could not have written
